newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian screen idol Mastroianni had lust for life.
newsitem.headline: Italian screen idol Mastroianni had lust for life.

text.p: Italian screen idol Marcello Mastroianni, who turned millions of women onto the thrill of the Latin Lover, was a down-to-earth man who took all life had to offer and hated the idea of death.
"I don't like the idea of dying at all," Mastroianni, who died in Paris on Thursday at the age of 72, told an interviewer last year before beginning his last theatre role.
"I haven't always been loyal, I admit. I could have applied myself more, done better. But between love and work, I've been very lucky. Maybe the secret is that I've loved life," he said.
Mastroianni shot to stardom in Federico Fellini's 1960 classic "La Dolce Vita" and acted in 160 films in a career spanning half a century.
"He was perhaps the greatest European cinema actor of the last 50 years," French producer Daniel Toscan du Plantier said.

Despite bouts of ill-health, Mastroianni had been working almost up to his death and had recently filmed a movie in Portugal and returned to theatre work in Italy in "Le Ultime Lune" (The Last Moons) by Italian dramatist Furio Bordon.
"The truth is that deep down inside, I still feel not only young, but almost a kid," he said before the play opened.
Italians adored "Il Bel Marcello" as he came to be known for his roles as seducer who always seemed to end up being seduced.

With Italian diva Sophia Loren, he portrayed Italian couples in 12 films including "Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" and "Marriage Italian Style". The pair's on-screen chemistry always kept everyone guessing about real life romance.

But he owed his career to Fellini, Italy's most famous film director, who gave him his break in "La Dolce Vita" even though the part of the suave reporter hero who chronicles decadant Rome life had originally been intended for Paul Newman.
Fellini was his confidant and mentor. The director, who died in 1993, described Mastroianni as his alter-ego.
Their professional relationship was cemented in the 1960s with films such as "Eight-and-a-Half" and continued into the 1980s with "City of Women", "Ginger e Fred" and "The Interview".
Mastroianni, bespectacled and dimpled, always portrayed himself as a shy boy who just got lucky in life and love.

"When I was a kid...I had a chest that looked like a basket and two bird's legs," Mastroianni said in 1967. "I'm not handsome and I never have been. I've got an ordinary face, even a country bumpkin's face."
Mastroianni's agent Giovanna Cau, a friend since the 1950s, said: "He was very simple, very discreet."
"He was an exceptional man," she told Reuters, her voice breaking with emotion.
Mastroianni, who shunned publicity and rarely granted interviews, was born to peasant parents on September 28, 1924, at Fontana Liri, a mountain hamlet southeast of Rome.
When he was still a boy the family moved to the northern industrial city of Turin and then to Rome, where he finished a degree in surveying and planned to become an architect.

When he was 19, he was picked up by Nazi troops who had occupied Rome and sent to a forced labour camp in northern Italy. He escaped to Venice, where he drew pictures of the lagoon city's landmarks and sold them to tourists for food.

After the war he returned to Rome, where he worked as a clerk in the accounting department of the British Eagle-Lion film company and in the evenings began acting with a Rome University theatrical company.
In 1947 he made his screen debut in the Italian version of "Les Miserables" and a year later made his stage debut in a play which starred Giulietta Masina, Fellini's wife.
Mastroianni tried to stay out of the public eye and rarely granted interviews, perhaps afraid the world was only interested in lurid details of his love life.
"I'll never speak of the most intimate, most secret things," he said recently.
He married his wife, Flora, after a brief romance and had a daughter, but ruled out divorce despite a string of affairs.
He has another daughter, the actress Chiara Mastroianni, from a relationship with French actress Catherine Deneuve.
